_licence: ORIGINAL connective wording, built around Casefile B's own document spine (Docs 6, 13, 14) and the unit plan's own framing of 1676 as the hinge year. No third-party text.
intro: Match each cause to its effect in the hardening of race-based slavery.

left.label: Fear of a poor-white/enslaved alliance, after 1676
The trade map listing enslaved people beside sugar and pepper (Document 6)

right.label: Same offense, three people — but the sentences stop matching; the split has already begun before 1676
Shows Virginia's elite what an alliance of poor whites and enslaved people can do
Colonial assemblies write law that splits servitude sharply by race
Enslaved people are treated as property in law and in commerce alike
Enslaved people are listed under the same heading as livestock and household goods

rationale.a: Document 13's own timeline: three separate rulings on the same kind of offense, but the sentences already stop lining up before 1676 — the pattern is bending, not yet split cleanly by race.
rationale.b: Bacon's Rebellion is the event the unit plan itself names as the hinge — it shows Virginia's elite the danger of poor whites and enslaved people making common cause.
rationale.c: That fear is what drives colonial assemblies, after 1676, to write law that divides servitude sharply along racial lines.
rationale.d: Document 6's trade map prints human beings in the same list as sugar and pepper — commerce treats people as goods, the same logic the law comes to treat them under.
rationale.e: Document 14's probate inventory lists enslaved people under the same heading as livestock and household goods — property in law, not just in commerce.
